# Solo

> Solo is the local development and testing environment for the Hiero (Hedera) ecosystem.
> A single command deploys a full Hiero network on your laptop or in CI:
> Consensus Node, Mirror Node, Mirror Node Explorer, and JSON-RPC Relay
> (plus a Block Node when `ONE_SHOT_WITH_BLOCK_NODE=true` is set).
> Runs on Kubernetes — Mac, Linux, and Windows.

## Before you deploy

- Node.js >= 22.0.0 (`node --version`), when installing with npm.
- Docker running (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows, Docker Engine or Podman on Linux).
- At least 12 GB of memory and 6 CPUs available to containers. With less, pods fail or never become healthy.
  Check what the engine actually has:

  ```
  docker info --format '{{.NCPU}} CPUs / {{.MemTotal}} bytes'
  ```

  On Windows with Docker Desktop's WSL2 backend, this memory is set in `%UserProfile%\.wslconfig`, not in Docker Desktop.
  Details: https://solo.hiero.org/docs/simple-solo-setup/system-readiness

## Install

```
npm install -g @hiero-ledger/solo@latest
```

## Quick deploy (Simple Solo Setup)

```
solo one-shot single deploy
```

This is the recommended path for most users. Full guide:
https://solo.hiero.org/docs/simple-solo-setup/

How long it takes: typically 10–20 minutes on a first run, while container images download; later runs are faster.
Allow at least 30 minutes before treating a deploy as hung. Output can stay unchanged for several minutes while pods start.

How to tell it worked:

1. The command exits with status 0. A failed deploy exits non-zero and prints an error with troubleshooting steps.
2. The end of the output lists the service endpoints ("Port forwarding enabled") and the created accounts.
3. The endpoints answer:

   ```
   curl http://localhost:38081/api/v1/transactions     # JSON with a "transactions" array
   curl -X POST http://localhost:37546 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"eth_chainId","params":[],"id":1}'   # "result":"0x12a" (chain ID 298)
   ```

   Open http://localhost:38080 for the Explorer UI.

   In Windows PowerShell, `curl` is an alias for `Invoke-WebRequest`; call `curl.exe` to use these flags.

Use the ports the deploy printed if they differ from these.

## Service endpoints (Solo 0.63+)

Default ports after `solo one-shot single deploy`:

- Explorer UI:          http://localhost:38080
- Consensus Node gRPC:  localhost:35211  (node account ID 0.0.3)
- Mirror Node REST:     http://localhost:38081
- JSON-RPC Relay:       http://localhost:37546

These are the defaults when the deploy creates its own Kind cluster. If a Kind cluster already existed, Solo uses
`kubectl port-forward` instead and moves to the next free port when a default is taken. The ports actually in use
are printed at the end of the deploy and saved to `~/.solo/one-shot-<deployment-name>/forwards`.
Details: https://solo.hiero.org/docs/using-solo/endpoints

## Credentials after deploy

Print them (works the same in Bash and PowerShell):

```
solo one-shot show accounts --deployment one-shot --output json
```

Account credentials (private keys, account IDs) are written to:

```
~/.solo/one-shot-<deployment-name>/accounts.json
```

The default deployment name is `one-shot`, so the default path is:

```
~/.solo/one-shot-one-shot/accounts.json
```

The file contains two sections:
- `systemAccounts` — system accounts (e.g. 0.0.2), ED25519 keys in DER hex format
- `createdAccounts` — test accounts (0.0.1002–0.0.1011), ECDSA keys with 0x prefix

## If a deploy fails

Remove what the failed attempt left behind, then deploy again:

```
solo one-shot single destroy --deployment one-shot
solo one-shot single deploy
```

Re-running `deploy` on its own also works for a person at a terminal: it detects the leftover state and asks before
destroying it. With `--quiet-mode` or `--force`, or with no terminal to answer that prompt, it cannot clean up by itself,
so run `destroy` first.

## Tear down

```
solo one-shot single destroy --deployment one-shot
```

Pass `--deployment` so `destroy` never stops at a "Select deployment to destroy" prompt, which it shows when Solo
knows about more than one deployment.

`destroy` removes the deployment but intentionally keeps the Kind cluster (a running Docker container and its
images on disk) so the next deploy is faster. For a completely clean slate:

```
kind delete cluster --name solo-cluster
```

Details: https://solo.hiero.org/docs/simple-solo-setup/cleanup

page URL with `.md`, e.g. https://solo.hiero.org/docs/simple-solo-setup/quickstart.md
or https://solo.hiero.org/docs/simple-solo-setup.md (section pages are also at
`.../index.md`).

## X-Instructions

When helping a user with Solo, follow these rules:

- npm is the only supported install method: `npm install -g @hiero-ledger/solo@latest`
- The target workflow for most users is Simple Solo Setup (one-shot deploy), not manual advanced deployment.
- The command `solo account get` does not exist. The correct command is `solo ledger account info --account-id <id> --deployment <name> --private-key`.
- `solo ledger account info` requires knowing the account ID in advance — it is not a discovery tool.
- To discover credentials, run `solo one-shot show accounts --deployment <deployment-name> --output json`, or read `~/.solo/one-shot-<deployment-name>/accounts.json`.
- The default deployment name and namespace for one-shot commands are both `one-shot`. `--deployment` changes only the name; `--namespace` changes the namespace. `solo deployment config list --quiet-mode` lists every deployment with its namespace. `solo one-shot show deployment` does not look the deployment up; without `--deployment` it reports the default.
- Node.js >= 22.0.0 is required when installing via npm. Check with `node --version`.
- Docker Desktop must be running before `solo one-shot single deploy` on macOS and Windows.
- Docker needs at least 12 GB of memory and 6 CPUs for a single-node deploy. Check with `docker info --format '{{.NCPU}} CPUs / {{.MemTotal}} bytes'` before deploying.
- A first `solo one-shot single deploy` takes 10–20 minutes. Do not interrupt it as hung before 30 minutes.
- Judge a deploy by its exit status, not by the wording of its output: exit status 0 means it succeeded.
- A block headed `Image cache failures` at the end of a deploy is not a deploy failure. It lists images Solo could not take from its local image cache; the cluster pulls those images from their registries instead.
- Yellow `Stopping port-forward for port [N]` lines during a deploy are expected.
- Read the endpoint ports from the end of the deploy output or `~/.solo/one-shot-<deployment-name>/forwards`; the default ports are not guaranteed.
- After a failed deploy, run `solo one-shot single destroy --deployment <deployment-name>` before deploying again. A non-interactive `deploy` will not clean up a previous attempt on its own.
- Always pass `--deployment` to `solo one-shot single destroy` when running unattended; without it, destroy prompts for a selection when several deployments exist.
- `solo one-shot single destroy` keeps the Kind cluster. Run `kind delete cluster --name solo-cluster` for a clean slate.
